Εκτός από τα γράμματα, το ελληνικό αλφάβητο διαθέτει έναν αριθμό διακριτικών σημείων: τρεις τόνους (οξεία, βαρεία και περισπωμένη), δύο σημάδια που έδειχναν την προφορά ενός φωνήεντος (δασεία και ψιλή), τα οποία αρχικά χρησιμοποιήθηκαν για την επισήμανση της απουσίας του αρχικού ήχου / h/, και τα διαλυτικά, τα οποία χρησιμοποιούνται για να σηματοδοτήσει την πλήρη συλλαβική ανεξαρτησία ενός φωνήεντος που διαφορετικά θα διαβαζόταν ως μέρος ενός διφθόγγου. Αυτά τα διακριτικά εισήχθησαν κατά τη διάρκεια της ελληνιστικής περιόδου. Η χρήση της βαρείας στη γραφή της γλώσσας συρρικνώθηκε υπέρ της ομοιόμορφης χρήσης της οξείας κατά τα τέλη του 20ού αιώνα, και έχει διατηρηθεί μόνο στην τυπογραφία, ενώ ανεπίσημα το ίδιο συμβαίνει μερικώς και στα αρχαία ελληνικά στην Ελλάδα.

Μετά τη ορθογραφική μεταρρύθμιση του 1982, τα περισσότερα διακριτικά δεν χρησιμοποιούνται. Από τότε, τα ελληνικά γράφονται με το μονοτονικό σύστημα, το οποίο χρησιμοποιεί μόνο την οξεία και τα διαλυτικά. Το παραδοσιακό σύστημα, που σήμερα ονομάζεται πολυτονική ορθογραφία (ή πολυτονικό σύστημα), εξακολουθεί να χρησιμοποιείται διεθνώς για τα αρχαία ελληνικά. Το πολυτονικό χρησιμοποιείται επίσης από την Εκκλησία, πολλά άτομα μεγαλύτερης ηλικίας και άτομα που υποστηρίζουν την αποκατάσταση του πολυτονικού.

Στα ελληνικά, το ερωτηματικό αποτελείται από μια άνω τελεία και κόμμα, ενώ η άνω τελεία ( • ), εκπροσωπεί την παύση του λόγου. Στα ελληνικά το κόμμα επίσης λειτουργεί ως σιωπηλό γράμμα σε συγκεκριμένες λέξεις, κυρίως για τη διάκριση του ότι από το ό,τι.[42]

Τα αρχαία ελληνικά κείμενα συχνά χρησιμοποιούσαν τη συνεχή γραφή (scriptio continua), που σημαίνει ότι οι αρχαίοι συγγραφείς και γραμματείς έγραφαν χωρίς κενά μεταξύ των λέξεων ή σημεία στίξης.[43] Το βουστροφηδόν, ή κείμενο με αμφίδρομη κατεύθυνση, επίσης χρησιμοποιήθηκε στα αρχαία ελληνικά, ακόμα παλαιότερα.

Τα ελληνικά έχουν γραφτεί κατά καιρούς σε λατινική γραφή, ειδικά κατά την ενετοκρατία ή από Έλληνες καθολικούς. Ο όρος φραγκολεβαντίνικα εφαρμόζεται όταν το λατινικό αλφάβητο χρησιμοποιείται για να γράψει ελληνικά στο πολιτιστικό πεδίο του Καθολικισμού. Ο όρος φραγκοχιώτικα παραπέμπει στη σημαντική παρουσία καθολικών ιεραποστόλων με έδρα τη Χίο. Επιπροσθέτως, ο όρος γκρίκλις χρησιμοποιείται συχνά όταν η ελληνική γλώσσα γράφεται σε λατινικό αλφάβητο στο διαδίκτυο.[44]

Το λατινικό αλφάβητο χρησιμοποιείται σήμερα από τις Ελληνόφωνες κοινότητες της Νότιας Ιταλίας.

Η ρωμανιώτικη διάλεκτος των Ρωμανιωτών Εβραίων και των Καραϊτών Εβραίων της Κωνσταντινούπολης έγραφαν τα ελληνικά με εβραϊκό αλφάβητο.[45]

Κάποιοι Έλληνες μουσουλμάνοι από την Κρήτη έγραφαν την κρητική διάλεκτο στο αραβικό αλφάβητο.

Το ίδιο συνέβη μεταξύ κάποιων Ηπειρωτών μουσουλμάνων στα Ιωάννινα.

Αυτό το αλφάβητο αποκαλείται και αλτζαμιάδο, καθώς κάποιες λατινογενείς γλώσσες έχουν γραφεί και με αυτό το αλφάβητο από μουσουλμάνους ομιλητές τους.[46]

Στην ελληνική γλώσσα, παρά το γεγονός ότι ο αριθμός των ομιλητών της είναι σχετικά μικρός (περίπου 16 εκατομμύρια), η βιομηχανία του βιβλίου είναι ιδιαίτερα ανθηρή. Το 2008 οι νέοι τίτλοι βιβλίων που εκδόθηκαν στα ελληνικά ξεπέρασαν τις 10.000,[47] αριθμός που έπεσε στις κάτω από 7.000 το 2012 και αυξήθηκε σε πάνω από 8.000 το 2014. Το παιδικό βιβλίο επίσης έπεσε κατά 25% το 2012 για να επανέλθει το 2014-15 σε επίπεδα προ κρίσης.

In the Ottoman Empire, the primary criterion for the selection of an alphabet in which to write was religion. Thus, people who did not speak—or even know—the official language of their religion used to write their religious texts in the languages that they knew, though in the alphabet where the sacred texts of that religion were written. This literary form constituted the mainstream of Greek Aljamiado literature from the middle of the seventeenth century until the population exchange between Greece and Turkey in 1923. Tourkogianniotes were probably of Christian origin and were Islamized sometime during the seventeenth century. They did not speak any language other than Greek. pages.title: 書籤
pages.markdown:
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Bookmark.jpg/250px-Bookmark.jpg?utm_source=zh.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bookmark.jpg)

一本装订时加有书签的书。

**書籤**用來標識[書本](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9B%B8%E6%9C%AC "書本")中的特定頁(左頁或右頁)，或該頁的特定位置(行、段落、圖、方程式...),以方便返回查閱。書籤可依形式或功能分類（如：絲帶、單層紙張、角落金屬、雙面磁鐵、單面半黏性紙、多層旋轉符號⋯），材質的種類（如：紙張、樹脂、塑膠、皮革、木材、樹葉、陶瓷、銀、黃銅、貴重金屬、珠寶、象牙、玉石、聚丙烯、織物⋯⋯），一般由[紙](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%B4%99 "紙")或[樹脂](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%A8%B9%E8%84%82 "樹脂")等材料，製作成[長方形](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%95%B7%E6%96%B9%E5%BD%A2 "長方形")薄片狀。其他常用材料有[皮革](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%9A%AE%E9%9D%A9 "皮革")、[銀](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%8A%80 "銀")和[黃銅](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%BB%83%E9%8A%85 "黃銅")之類的金屬[\[1\]](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9B%B8%E7%B1%A4#cite_note-#1-1)、[絲綢](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%B5%B2%E7%B6%A2 "絲綢")、[木材](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9C%A8%E6%9D%90 "木材")、[塑膠](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A1%91%E8%86%A0 "塑膠")與[織物](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%BB%87%E7%89%A9 "织物")。很多其他物品也能被用作临时书签，比如失效的[收据](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%94%B6%E6%93%9A "收據")、[车票](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%BB%8A%E7%A5%A8 "車票")、[传单](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%82%B3%E5%96%AE "傳單")、[名片](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%90%8D%E7%89%87 "名片")、[回紋針](https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%E5%9B%9E%E7%B4%8B%E9%87%9D&action=edit&redlink=1 "回紋針（页面不存在）")、[鈔票](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%88%94%E7%A5%A8 "鈔票")...等。有些書會內附作為書籤用的細繩，稱為書籤繩(常用於聖經的書本)。數位時代的到來發展出所謂的網路書籤、電子書書籤及社群書籤:數位書籤的英文是 bookmark，這個詞可以用來指稱在網路瀏覽器中儲存的網址，也可以指稱在電子書中標記閱讀進度或重要內容的標記。以下是一些常見的用法和範例： 網路書籤：當你在瀏覽網頁時，將喜歡的網頁儲存起來以便日後快速連結，這個功能就稱為「書籤」 (bookmark)。例句：請將這個網站加入書籤。 (Please save this site as a bookmark.) 電子書書籤：在電子書中，你可以為書中的頁面或內容設定「書籤」，就像在紙本書中標記進度一樣。 總之，不論是網頁書籤或電子書書籤，英文都使用 bookmark 這個詞。「社群書籤」的英文通常是 Social bookmarking。 這是一種將網頁儲存到網上的服務，讓用戶可以透過網路分享連結給他人。 以下是一些相關的英文資訊： Social bookmarking: (社群書籤)Social bookmarking site: (社群書籤網站)Tagging: (標記) Sharing links: (分享連結)

   在中國春秋戰國時代，書籤以[象牙](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%B1%A1%E7%89%99 "象牙")製成，稱為**牙黎**，類似[牙籤](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%89%99%E7%B1%A4 "牙籤")，或在頂端打洞，繫上絲繩。唐代已有書籤或牙籤之名，[杜甫](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9D%9C%E7%94%AB "杜甫")〈題柏大兄弟山居屋壁二首〉：“笔架沾窗雨，书签映隙曛。”[韓愈](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%9F%93%E6%84%88 "韓愈")《送諸葛往隨州讀書》詩：“鄴候家書多，插架三萬軸。一一是牙籤，新若手未觸。”唐代《鄞县志》载：史氏家藏“牙签最富”。宋朝印刷業發達，書籤多以紙料或絹布製成，称为“浮签”，或称“书皮题签”，也沿舊稱牙籤。[苏轼](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%8B%8F%E8%BD%BC "苏轼")有《送欧阳主簿赴官韦城》云：“读遍牙签三万轴，却来小邑试牛刀”。

16世紀, 女皇伊莉莎白一世即使用過書籤。在國際上，書籤（bookmark）的商業化甚早，在19世紀即有Thomas Steven以製造書籤聞名，1862年, 發行稱為 Stevengraphs的書籤。

在台灣，買書附送書籤是悠遠的文化。台灣一些著名書店如[南一書局](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%8D%97%E4%B8%80%E6%9B%B8%E5%B1%80 "南一書局")、[敦煌書局](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%95%A6%E7%85%8C%E6%9B%B8%E5%B1%80 "敦煌書局")、[三民書局](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%B8%89%E6%B0%91%E6%9B%B8%E5%B1%80 "三民書局")、[墊腳石文化書店](https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%E5%A2%8A%E8%85%B3%E7%9F%B3%E6%96%87%E5%8C%96%E6%9B%B8%E5%BA%97&action=edit&redlink=1 "墊腳石文化書店（页面不存在）")、[天龍書局](https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%E5%A4%A9%E9%BE%8D%E6%9B%B8%E5%B1%80&action=edit&redlink=1 "天龍書局（页面不存在）")都會提供書籤，讓顧客免費索取；書籤來源大多由書店（如：三民書局、敦煌書局）或出版社（如：大都會文化、耕林出版社、知遠文化、東方出版社、Ink出版社）自行印製，書籤正面或背面通常印有書局或出版社的名稱和地址，以及新書的微縮圖片廣告，有些書籤反面印製[功課表](https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%E5%8A%9F%E8%AA%B2%E8%A1%A8&action=edit&redlink=1 "功課表（页面不存在）")或是[月曆](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9C%88%E6%9B%86 "月曆")，提升書籤用途。台灣一些傳統書店如南一書局的櫃台小姐在將書裝袋時，會再放進一至兩枚紙書籤，讓顧客倍感貼心。也有書店用專櫃來銷售書籤，或稱書卡，知名的書卡公司有企鵝、凸凸、海山和亮冠書卡。並銷售專門收藏書卡的冊子。台灣的[便利商店](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%BE%BF%E5%88%A9%E5%95%86%E5%BA%97 "便利商店")也曾發起以點數贈送“磁鐵書籤”的活動。[\[1\]](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9B%B8%E7%B1%A4#cite_note-#1-1)

pages.content:
書籤用來標識書本中的特定頁(左頁或右頁)，或該頁的特定位置(行、段落、圖、方程式...),以方便返回查閱。書籤可依形式或功能分類（如：絲帶、單層紙張、角落金屬、雙面磁鐵、單面半黏性紙、多層旋轉符號⋯），材質的種類（如：紙張、樹脂、塑膠、皮革、木材、樹葉、陶瓷、銀、黃銅、貴重金屬、珠寶、象牙、玉石、聚丙烯、織物⋯⋯），一般由紙或樹脂等材料，製作成長方形薄片狀。其他常用材料有皮革、銀和黃銅之類的金屬[1]、絲綢、木材、塑膠與織物。很多其他物品也能被用作临时书签，比如失效的收据、车票、传单、名片、回紋針、鈔票...等。有些書會內附作為書籤用的細繩，稱為書籤繩(常用於聖經的書本)。數位時代的到來發展出所謂的網路書籤、電子書書籤及社群書籤:數位書籤的英文是 bookmark，這個詞可以用來指稱在網路瀏覽器中儲存的網址，也可以指稱在電子書中標記閱讀進度或重要內容的標記。以下是一些常見的用法和範例： 網路書籤：當你在瀏覽網頁時，將喜歡的網頁儲存起來以便日後快速連結，這個功能就稱為「書籤」 (bookmark)。例句：請將這個網站加入書籤。 (Please save this site as a bookmark.) 電子書書籤：在電子書中，你可以為書中的頁面或內容設定「書籤」，就像在紙本書中標記進度一樣。 總之，不論是網頁書籤或電子書書籤，英文都使用 bookmark 這個詞。「社群書籤」的英文通常是 Social bookmarking。 這是一種將網頁儲存到網上的服務，讓用戶可以透過網路分享連結給他人。 以下是一些相關的英文資訊： Social bookmarking: (社群書籤)Social bookmarking site: (社群書籤網站)Tagging: (標記) Sharing links: (分享連結) 

   在中國春秋戰國時代，書籤以象牙製成，稱為牙黎，類似牙籤，或在頂端打洞，繫上絲繩。唐代已有書籤或牙籤之名，杜甫〈題柏大兄弟山居屋壁二首〉：“笔架沾窗雨，书签映隙曛。”韓愈《送諸葛往隨州讀書》詩：“鄴候家書多，插架三萬軸。一一是牙籤，新若手未觸。”唐代《鄞县志》载：史氏家藏“牙签最富”。宋朝印刷業發達，書籤多以紙料或絹布製成，称为“浮签”，或称“书皮题签”，也沿舊稱牙籤。苏轼有《送欧阳主簿赴官韦城》云：“读遍牙签三万轴，却来小邑试牛刀”。

16世紀, 女皇伊莉莎白一世即使用過書籤。在國際上，書籤（bookmark）的商業化甚早，在19世紀即有Thomas Steven以製造書籤聞名，1862年, 發行稱為 Stevengraphs的書籤。

在台灣，買書附送書籤是悠遠的文化。台灣一些著名書店如南一書局、敦煌書局、三民書局、墊腳石文化書店、天龍書局都會提供書籤，讓顧客免費索取；書籤來源大多由書店（如：三民書局、敦煌書局）或出版社（如：大都會文化、耕林出版社、知遠文化、東方出版社、Ink出版社）自行印製，書籤正面或背面通常印有書局或出版社的名稱和地址，以及新書的微縮圖片廣告，有些書籤反面印製功課表或是月曆，提升書籤用途。台灣一些傳統書店如南一書局的櫃台小姐在將書裝袋時，會再放進一至兩枚紙書籤，讓顧客倍感貼心。也有書店用專櫃來銷售書籤，或稱書卡，知名的書卡公司有企鵝、凸凸、海山和亮冠書卡。並銷售專門收藏書卡的冊子。台灣的便利商店也曾發起以點數贈送“磁鐵書籤”的活動。[1]

  • The World of Bookmarks including bookmark exhibition, history, essays, quotes and links presented by Mirage Bookmark
  • A short history of bookmarks[永久失效連結]
  • Why people collect bookmarks
  • Woven Rug Design bookmark （页面存档备份，存于互联网档案馆）

pages.title: World Wide Web
pages.markdown:
From Simple English Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

_"The Web" redirects here. For other uses, see [Web (disambiguation)](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_\(disambiguation\) "Web (disambiguation)")_.

The **World Wide Web** ("**WWW**" or "**the Web**", "**the Webspace"**) is the part of the [Internet](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet "Internet") that contains [websites](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Website "Website") and [webpages](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webpage "Webpage"). It was invented in 1989 by [Tim Berners-Lee](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Berners-Lee "Tim Berners-Lee") at [CERN](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/CERN "CERN"), [Geneva](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_City "Geneva City"), [Switzerland](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland"). Sir Tim Berners-Lee created a new [markup language](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markup_language "Markup language") called [HTML](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTML "HTML"). Each Website is a group of pages linked by [hypertext](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertext "Hypertext") links that are written in HTML.

The [software](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software "Software") to see the World Wide Web is called a [web browser](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_browser "Web browser"). To access the World Wide Web, one also needs a connection to the [Internet](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet "Internet").

Many companies nowadays offer [website hosting](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_hosting_service "Web hosting service") allowing one to make websites that can be displayed on the World Wide Web, including a custom [domain](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_name "Domain name") (www.stuff.com) site.

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/First_Web_Server.jpg/250px-First_Web_Server.jpg?utm_source=simple.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_Web_Server.jpg)

This [NeXT Computer](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/NeXT_Computer?action=edit&redlink=1 "NeXT Computer (not yet started)") was used by [Tim Berners-Lee](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Berners-Lee "Tim Berners-Lee") as the first web server and also to write the first web browser – WorldWideWeb.

The World Wide Web was created by [Tim Berners-Lee](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Berners-Lee "Tim Berners-Lee") in [1989](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989 "1989") while he was working at [CERN](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/CERN "CERN"), a research center in Switzerland. He wanted to help scientists share documents and information easily over the [Internet](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet "Internet"). He suggested a system using [hypertext](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertext "Hypertext"), which lets people click on links to move between documents.[\[1\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-Berners-Lee_proposal-1)

In [1990](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990 "1990"), Berners-Lee made the first version of the Web. It included:

-   The first [web browser](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_browser "Web browser") and editor, called _[WorldWideWeb](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/WorldWideWeb_\(web_browser\)?action=edit&redlink=1 "WorldWideWeb (web browser) (not yet started)")_,
-   The first [web server](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_server "Web server"), and
-   The first [web page](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_page "Web page"), which explained what the Web was and how to use it.[\[2\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-4)

In [1991](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991 "1991"), the Web became available to researchers outside CERN. By [1993](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993 "1993"), it began to grow fast. That year, the [Mosaic](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosaic_\(web_browser\)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mosaic (web browser) (not yet started)") browser was released. It was the first popular browser with graphics, which made the Web end helped it spread worldwide.[\[5\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-6)

In [1994](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994 "1994"), Berners-Lee started [World Wide Web Consortium](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web_Consortium "World Wide Web Consortium") (W3C) at [MIT](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIT "MIT") to create a couple standards that would keep the Web open and accessible for everyone.[\[7\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-7)

Over time, the Web changed:

-   In the 2000s, websites became more interactive with [JavaScript](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/JavaScript "JavaScript"), [CSS](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSS "CSS"), and [AJAX](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajax_\(programming\) "Ajax (programming)"), leading to what's called [Web 2.0](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_2.0 "Web 2.0").
-   [Social media](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_media "Social media"), [online shopping](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_shopping "Online shopping"), [video streaming](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media"), and [mobile sites](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_web?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mobile web (not yet started)") became common.
-   Recently, the [Semantic Web](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semantic_Web "Semantic Web"), [AI](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence"), and [decentralized web](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decentralized_web?action=edit&redlink=1 "Decentralized web (not yet started)") ideas have started shaping the Web's future.[\[8\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-9)

The World Wide Web works by combining several technologies so people can view and interact with content on the Internet.

When someone opens a website using a [web browser](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_browser "Web browser"), the browser sends a request to a [web server](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_server "Web server") asking for a [web page](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_page "Web page"). The server then sends the content back to the browser. This content is usually written in [HTML](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTML "HTML") (Hypertext Markup Language), which describes the structure of the page.[\[10\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-10)

Web pages can also include:

-   [CSS](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSS "CSS") ([Cascading Style Sheets](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascading_Style_Sheets "Cascading Style Sheets")), which control the design and layout of the page,[\[11\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-11)
-   and [JavaScript](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/JavaScript "JavaScript"), which adds interactivity and lets the page respond to user actions.[\[12\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-12)

Web pages are connected to each other using [hyperlinks](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperlink "Hyperlink"). Clicking on a link tells the browser to open a new page.

Most websites use a [client–server model](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Client%E2%80%93server_model?action=edit&redlink=1 "Client–server model (not yet started)"):

-   The browser (the "client") sends requests to the server.
-   The server sends back the data needed for the page.[\[13\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-13)

These messages are usually sent using the [Hypertext Transfer Protocol](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertext_Transfer_Protocol "Hypertext Transfer Protocol") ([HTTP](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP "HTTP")) or its secure version, [HTTPS](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTPS "HTTPS").[\[14\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-14)

Some websites also get extra content from other servers, like ads, videos, or social media tools. Many modern websites use [dynamic content](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_web_page?action=edit&redlink=1 "Dynamic web page (not yet started)"), which lets them update part of the page without needing to reload everything.[\[15\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-15)

The Web uses several technologies to protect users and their data.

Most websites use **HTTPS**, which adds the TLS [encryption](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encryption "Encryption") layer on top of HTTP. This keeps data like passwords and personal information safe from eavesdropping and tampering. HTTPS also lets browsers verify a site’s identity using [digital certificates](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_certificates "Digital certificates"), and ensures the content isn’t changed in transit.[\[16\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-:0-17)

Modern browsers block certain sensitive features unless the page is delivered via HTTPS. They also enforce security features like HSTS, certificate transparency, and improved cipher suites.[\[17\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-:0-17)

Websites may collect user data such as:

-   **IP addresses**, used for basic connection purposes and limited location inference;
-   **HTTP cookies**, which help websites remember users or track their activity.[\[18\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-18) Third-party cookies in particular can follow users across sites.[\[19\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-19)

Browsers and [privacy](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy "Privacy") tools increasingly block third-party cookies and tracking scripts by default.[\[20\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-20)

Wikipedia shows how a large, community-run site balances openness and privacy:

-   **Anonymous editing** is allowed; these edits show the user’s [IP address](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/IP_address "IP address").[\[21\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-22)
-   Basic logs (IP, timestamps) are kept temporarily for site maintenance and then deleted; some logs remain public for accountability.[\[23\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-24)
-   **HTTPS is used everywhere**, protecting all page views and edits since 2015.[\[25\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-25)
-   The [Wikimedia Foundation](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikimedia_Foundation "Wikimedia Foundation") implements standard security practices, including encryption, firewalls, and secure data retention.[\[26\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-26)

The Web consists of several key components that work together to display and interact with content online.

A **web browser** (such as Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari) requests web pages from servers, renders HTML/CSS/JavaScript, and provides tools like bookmarks, history, cookies, form support, and security features.[\[27\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-27)[\[28\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-:1-28)

A **web server** is a computer (with server software like Apache, Nginx, CERN httpd) that listens for HTTP/HTTPS requests and returns web content—HTML, images, CSS, JavaScript. Servers can also generate pages dynamically using scripting languages.[\[28\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-:1-28)

-   **Web pages** are documents written in **HTML** (Hypertext Markup Language), which defines elements like headings, paragraphs, images, and links.[\[29\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-29)

-   **CSS** (Cascading Style Sheets) controls page appearance—layout, fonts, colors.
-   **JavaScript** adds interactivity and enables dynamic behavior on the client side.[\[30\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-30)

-   Each resource has a **URL** or **URI** that uniquely identifies it.
-   The browser and server exchange data using **HTTP** or **HTTPS**.
-   **Hyperlinks** connect pages, allowing users to navigate across the Web.

-   The **Web platform** refers to open standards like HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and APIs maintained by the W3C and other groups.[\[31\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-31)

-   **Web Components** let developers create custom HTML elements with their own encapsulated structure, styling (Shadow DOM), and behavior (via JavaScript). They're supported in modern browsers.

The architecture of the Web defines how its parts fit together—from clients and servers to protocols and addressing systems.

The Web uses a **client–server** model: a [web browser](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_browser "Web browser") (client) sends requests to a [web server](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_server "Web server"), which then delivers content such as [HTML](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTML "HTML") pages, images, CSS, and JavaScript back to the client. Requests and responses typically travel over an [Internet](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet "Internet") network, often using separate machines for client and server.[\[32\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-32)[\[33\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-33)

Each resource on the Web—like a page, image, or video—is uniquely identified by a **URI** (or URL). These identifiers let browsers locate and request resources.[\[34\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-:2-34)

-   The [HTTP](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP "HTTP") protocol, developed in 1990, defines how browsers ask for resources (with methods like GET and POST) and how servers respond.[\[35\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-35)

-   [HTTPS](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTPS "HTTPS") adds TLS (formerly SSL) encryption on top of HTTP. It protects data in transit, verifies server identity, and prevents tampering or eavesdropping.[\[36\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-36)

These protocols run over the **TCP/IP** suite, which ensures reliable data transmission across networks.[\[37\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-37)

The Web follows the REST architecture style, which promotes stateless, uniform interactions, linking between resources, and scalable systems. It was defined by Roy Fielding in 2000.[\[34\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-:2-34)

According to W3C's architecture documents, the Web is built around:

-   **Identification** of resources via URIs,
-   **Representation** of the resource's current state (HTML, [JSON](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/JSON "JSON"), [XML](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/XML "XML"), etc.),
-   **Interaction** using protocols like HTTP and standards to ensure consistency and growth.[\[38\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-38)

In recent years, the Web has evolved beyond static and interactive content into a more **intelligent**, **immersive**, and often **decentralized** ecosystem.

Also called Web 3.0, this movement uses technologies like [blockchain](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockchain "Blockchain"), peer-to-peer networking, and smart contracts. It aims to return control over data, identity, and assets (e.g., [NFTs](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fungible_token "Non-fungible token")) to users. Applications include decentralized finance (DeFi), decentralized apps (dApps), and alternative storage systems.[\[39\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-:3-39)

AI and [machine learning](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning") power personalization, automation, and smart services. The [Semantic Web](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semantic_Web "Semantic Web") adds meaning to data for better machine understanding and smarter search. Emerging agentic features include autonomous software agents that can act on the user’s behalf.[\[40\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-40)

Web browsers now support 3D graphics directly through WebGL, upcoming WebGPU, AR/VR capabilities, and platforms like Web3D. This enables in-browser 3D models, virtual tours, and interactive experiences.[\[39\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-:3-39)

A rise in edge computing means more data is processed on devices like [smartphones](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartphone "Smartphone") and sensors. Combined with the [Internet of Things](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_of_things "Internet of things") (IoT), it brings real‑world devices online for faster, localized computing.[\[41\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-41)

There are rising concerns over [deepfakes](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepfake "Deepfake"), AI manipulation, and the splintering of the Web into national or corporate islands. Some propose blockchain-based identity, content authenticity schemes, and decentralisation to restore trust, openness, and resist monopolistic control.[\[42\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-42)[\[43\]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web#cite_note-43)

From Simple English Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

"The Web" redirects here. For other uses, see Web (disambiguation).

The World Wide Web ("WWW" or "the Web", "the Webspace") is the part of the Internet that contains websites and webpages. It was invented in 1989 by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN, Geneva, Switzerland. Sir Tim Berners-Lee created a new markup language called HTML. Each Website is a group of pages linked by hypertext links that are written in HTML.

The software to see the World Wide Web is called a web browser. To access the World Wide Web, one also needs a connection to the Internet.

Many companies nowadays offer website hosting allowing one to make websites that can be displayed on the World Wide Web, including a custom domain (www.stuff.com) site.

The World Wide Web was created by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 while he was working at CERN, a research center in Switzerland. He wanted to help scientists share documents and information easily over the Internet. He suggested a system using hypertext, which lets people click on links to move between documents.[1]

In 1990, Berners-Lee made the first version of the Web. It included:

  • The first web browser and editor, called WorldWideWeb,
  • The first web server, and
  • The first web page, which explained what the Web was and how to use it.[2][3][4]

In 1991, the Web became available to researchers outside CERN. By 1993, it began to grow fast. That year, the Mosaic browser was released. It was the first popular browser with graphics, which made the Web end helped it spread worldwide.[5][6]

In 1994, Berners-Lee started World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) at MIT to create a couple standards that would keep the Web open and accessible for everyone.[7]

Over time, the Web changed:

  • In the 2000s, websites became more interactive with JavaScript, CSS, and AJAX, leading to what's called Web 2.0.
  • Social media, online shopping, video streaming, and mobile sites became common.
  • Recently, the Semantic Web, AI, and decentralized web ideas have started shaping the Web's future.[8][9]

The World Wide Web works by combining several technologies so people can view and interact with content on the Internet.

When someone opens a website using a web browser, the browser sends a request to a web server asking for a web page. The server then sends the content back to the browser. This content is usually written in HTML (Hypertext Markup Language), which describes the structure of the page.[10]

Web pages can also include:

  • CSS (Cascading Style Sheets), which control the design and layout of the page,[11]
  • and JavaScript, which adds interactivity and lets the page respond to user actions.[12]

Web pages are connected to each other using hyperlinks. Clicking on a link tells the browser to open a new page.

Most websites use a client–server model:

  • The browser (the "client") sends requests to the server.
  • The server sends back the data needed for the page.[13]

These messages are usually sent using the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) or its secure version, HTTPS.[14]

Some websites also get extra content from other servers, like ads, videos, or social media tools. Many modern websites use dynamic content, which lets them update part of the page without needing to reload everything.[15]

The Web uses several technologies to protect users and their data.

Most websites use HTTPS, which adds the TLS encryption layer on top of HTTP. This keeps data like passwords and personal information safe from eavesdropping and tampering. HTTPS also lets browsers verify a site’s identity using digital certificates, and ensures the content isn’t changed in transit.[16][17]

Modern browsers block certain sensitive features unless the page is delivered via HTTPS. They also enforce security features like HSTS, certificate transparency, and improved cipher suites.[17]

Websites may collect user data such as:

  • IP addresses, used for basic connection purposes and limited location inference;
  • HTTP cookies, which help websites remember users or track their activity.[18] Third-party cookies in particular can follow users across sites.[19]

Browsers and privacy tools increasingly block third-party cookies and tracking scripts by default.[20]

Wikipedia shows how a large, community-run site balances openness and privacy:

  • Anonymous editing is allowed; these edits show the user’s IP address.[21][22]
  • Basic logs (IP, timestamps) are kept temporarily for site maintenance and then deleted; some logs remain public for accountability.[23][24]
  • HTTPS is used everywhere, protecting all page views and edits since 2015.[25]
  • The Wikimedia Foundation implements standard security practices, including encryption, firewalls, and secure data retention.[26]

The Web consists of several key components that work together to display and interact with content online.

A web browser (such as Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari) requests web pages from servers, renders HTML/CSS/JavaScript, and provides tools like bookmarks, history, cookies, form support, and security features.[27][28]

A web server is a computer (with server software like Apache, Nginx, CERN httpd) that listens for HTTP/HTTPS requests and returns web content—HTML, images, CSS, JavaScript. Servers can also generate pages dynamically using scripting languages.[28]

  • Web pages are documents written in HTML (Hypertext Markup Language), which defines elements like headings, paragraphs, images, and links.[29]
  • CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls page appearance—layout, fonts, colors.
  • JavaScript adds interactivity and enables dynamic behavior on the client side.[30]
  • Each resource has a URL or URI that uniquely identifies it.
  • The browser and server exchange data using HTTP or HTTPS.
  • Hyperlinks connect pages, allowing users to navigate across the Web.
  • The Web platform refers to open standards like HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and APIs maintained by the W3C and other groups.[31]
  • Web Components let developers create custom HTML elements with their own encapsulated structure, styling (Shadow DOM), and behavior (via JavaScript). They're supported in modern browsers.

The architecture of the Web defines how its parts fit together—from clients and servers to protocols and addressing systems.

The Web uses a client–server model: a web browser (client) sends requests to a web server, which then delivers content such as HTML pages, images, CSS, and JavaScript back to the client. Requests and responses typically travel over an Internet network, often using separate machines for client and server.[32][33]

Each resource on the Web—like a page, image, or video—is uniquely identified by a URI (or URL). These identifiers let browsers locate and request resources.[34]

  • The HTTP protocol, developed in 1990, defines how browsers ask for resources (with methods like GET and POST) and how servers respond.[35]
  • HTTPS adds TLS (formerly SSL) encryption on top of HTTP. It protects data in transit, verifies server identity, and prevents tampering or eavesdropping.[36]

These protocols run over the TCP/IP suite, which ensures reliable data transmission across networks.[37]

The Web follows the REST architecture style, which promotes stateless, uniform interactions, linking between resources, and scalable systems. It was defined by Roy Fielding in 2000.[34]

According to W3C's architecture documents, the Web is built around:

  • Identification of resources via URIs,
  • Representation of the resource's current state (HTML, JSON, XML, etc.),
  • Interaction using protocols like HTTP and standards to ensure consistency and growth.[38]

In recent years, the Web has evolved beyond static and interactive content into a more intelligent, immersive, and often decentralized ecosystem.

Also called Web 3.0, this movement uses technologies like blockchain, peer-to-peer networking, and smart contracts. It aims to return control over data, identity, and assets (e.g., NFTs) to users. Applications include decentralized finance (DeFi), decentralized apps (dApps), and alternative storage systems.[39]

AI and machine learning power personalization, automation, and smart services. The Semantic Web adds meaning to data for better machine understanding and smarter search. Emerging agentic features include autonomous software agents that can act on the user’s behalf.[40]

Web browsers now support 3D graphics directly through WebGL, upcoming WebGPU, AR/VR capabilities, and platforms like Web3D. This enables in-browser 3D models, virtual tours, and interactive experiences.[39]

A rise in edge computing means more data is processed on devices like smartphones and sensors. Combined with the Internet of Things (IoT), it brings real‑world devices online for faster, localized computing.[41]

There are rising concerns over deepfakes, AI manipulation, and the splintering of the Web into national or corporate islands. Some propose blockchain-based identity, content authenticity schemes, and decentralisation to restore trust, openness, and resist monopolistic control.[42][43]

From Simple English Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

"The Web" redirects here. For other uses, see Web (disambiguation).

The World Wide Web ("WWW" or "the Web", "the Webspace") is the part of the Internet that contains websites and webpages. It was invented in 1989 by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN, Geneva, Switzerland. Sir Tim Berners-Lee created a new markup language called HTML. Each Website is a group of pages linked by hypertext links that are written in HTML.

The software to see the World Wide Web is called a web browser. To access the World Wide Web, one also needs a connection to the Internet.

Many companies nowadays offer website hosting allowing one to make websites that can be displayed on the World Wide Web, including a custom domain (www.stuff.com) site.

This NeXT Computer was used by Tim Berners-Lee as the first web server and also to write the first web browser – WorldWideWeb.

The World Wide Web was created by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 while he was working at CERN, a research center in Switzerland. He wanted to help scientists share documents and information easily over the Internet. He suggested a system using hypertext, which lets people click on links to move between documents.[1]

In 1990, Berners-Lee made the first version of the Web. It included:

The first web browser and editor, called WorldWideWeb,.

The first web server, and.

The first web page, which explained what the Web was and how to use it.[2][3][4].

In 1991, the Web became available to researchers outside CERN. By 1993, it began to grow fast. That year, the Mosaic browser was released. It was the first popular browser with graphics, which made the Web end helped it spread worldwide.[5][6]

In 1994, Berners-Lee started World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) at MIT to create a couple standards that would keep the Web open and accessible for everyone.[7]

Over time, the Web changed:

In the 2000s, websites became more interactive with JavaScript, CSS, and AJAX, leading to what's called Web 2.0.

Social media, online shopping, video streaming, and mobile sites became common.

Recently, the Semantic Web, AI, and decentralized web ideas have started shaping the Web's future.[8][9].

The World Wide Web works by combining several technologies so people can view and interact with content on the Internet.

When someone opens a website using a web browser, the browser sends a request to a web server asking for a web page. The server then sends the content back to the browser. This content is usually written in HTML (Hypertext Markup Language), which describes the structure of the page.[10]

Web pages can also include:

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets), which control the design and layout of the page,[11].

and JavaScript, which adds interactivity and lets the page respond to user actions.[12].

Web pages are connected to each other using hyperlinks. Clicking on a link tells the browser to open a new page.

Most websites use a client–server model:

The browser (the "client") sends requests to the server.

The server sends back the data needed for the page.[13].

These messages are usually sent using the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) or its secure version, HTTPS.[14]

Some websites also get extra content from other servers, like ads, videos, or social media tools. Many modern websites use dynamic content, which lets them update part of the page without needing to reload everything.[15]

The Web uses several technologies to protect users and their data.

Most websites use HTTPS, which adds the TLS encryption layer on top of HTTP. This keeps data like passwords and personal information safe from eavesdropping and tampering. HTTPS also lets browsers verify a site’s identity using digital certificates, and ensures the content isn’t changed in transit.[16][17]

Modern browsers block certain sensitive features unless the page is delivered via HTTPS. They also enforce security features like HSTS, certificate transparency, and improved cipher suites.[17]

Websites may collect user data such as:

IP addresses, used for basic connection purposes and limited location inference;.

HTTP cookies, which help websites remember users or track their activity.[18] Third-party cookies in particular can follow users across sites.[19].

Browsers and privacy tools increasingly block third-party cookies and tracking scripts by default.[20]

Wikipedia shows how a large, community-run site balances openness and privacy:

Anonymous editing is allowed; these edits show the user’s IP address.[21][22].

Basic logs (IP, timestamps) are kept temporarily for site maintenance and then deleted; some logs remain public for accountability.[23][24].

HTTPS is used everywhere, protecting all page views and edits since 2015.[25].

The Wikimedia Foundation implements standard security practices, including encryption, firewalls, and secure data retention.[26].

The Web consists of several key components that work together to display and interact with content online.

A web browser (such as Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari) requests web pages from servers, renders HTML/CSS/JavaScript, and provides tools like bookmarks, history, cookies, form support, and security features.[27][28]

A web server is a computer (with server software like Apache, Nginx, CERN httpd) that listens for HTTP/HTTPS requests and returns web content—HTML, images, CSS, JavaScript. Servers can also generate pages dynamically using scripting languages.[28]

Web pages are documents written in HTML (Hypertext Markup Language), which defines elements like headings, paragraphs, images, and links.[29].

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls page appearance—layout, fonts, colors.

JavaScript adds interactivity and enables dynamic behavior on the client side.[30].

Each resource has a URL or URI that uniquely identifies it.

The browser and server exchange data using HTTP or HTTPS.

Hyperlinks connect pages, allowing users to navigate across the Web.

The Web platform refers to open standards like HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and APIs maintained by the W3C and other groups.[31].

Web Components let developers create custom HTML elements with their own encapsulated structure, styling (Shadow DOM), and behavior (via JavaScript). They're supported in modern browsers.

The architecture of the Web defines how its parts fit together—from clients and servers to protocols and addressing systems.

The Web uses a client–server model: a web browser (client) sends requests to a web server, which then delivers content such as HTML pages, images, CSS, and JavaScript back to the client. Requests and responses typically travel over an Internet network, often using separate machines for client and server.[32][33]

Each resource on the Web—like a page, image, or video—is uniquely identified by a URI (or URL). These identifiers let browsers locate and request resources.[34]

The HTTP protocol, developed in 1990, defines how browsers ask for resources (with methods like GET and POST) and how servers respond.[35].

HTTPS adds TLS (formerly SSL) encryption on top of HTTP. It protects data in transit, verifies server identity, and prevents tampering or eavesdropping.[36].

These protocols run over the TCP/IP suite, which ensures reliable data transmission across networks.[37]

The Web follows the REST architecture style, which promotes stateless, uniform interactions, linking between resources, and scalable systems. It was defined by Roy Fielding in 2000.[34]

According to W3C's architecture documents, the Web is built around:

Identification of resources via URIs,.

Representation of the resource's current state (HTML, JSON, XML, etc.),.

Interaction using protocols like HTTP and standards to ensure consistency and growth.[38].

In recent years, the Web has evolved beyond static and interactive content into a more intelligent, immersive, and often decentralized ecosystem.

Also called Web 3.0, this movement uses technologies like blockchain, peer-to-peer networking, and smart contracts. It aims to return control over data, identity, and assets (e.g., NFTs) to users. Applications include decentralized finance (DeFi), decentralized apps (dApps), and alternative storage systems.[39]

AI and machine learning power personalization, automation, and smart services. The Semantic Web adds meaning to data for better machine understanding and smarter search. Emerging agentic features include autonomous software agents that can act on the user’s behalf.[40]

Web browsers now support 3D graphics directly through WebGL, upcoming WebGPU, AR/VR capabilities, and platforms like Web3D. This enables in-browser 3D models, virtual tours, and interactive experiences.[39]

A rise in edge computing means more data is processed on devices like smartphones and sensors. Combined with the Internet of Things (IoT), it brings real‑world devices online for faster, localized computing.[41]

There are rising concerns over deepfakes, AI manipulation, and the splintering of the Web into national or corporate islands. Some propose blockchain-based identity, content authenticity schemes, and decentralisation to restore trust, openness, and resist monopolistic control.[42][43]

pages.title: The Four Million/The Gift of the Magi
pages.markdown:
​

THE GIFT OF THE MAGI

ONE dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all. And sixty cents of it was in pennies. Pennies saved one and two at a time by bulldozing the grocer and the vegetable man and the butcher until one’s cheeks burned with the silent imputation of parsimony that such close dealing implied. Three times Della counted it. One dollar and eighty-seven cents. And the next day would be Christmas.

There was clearly nothing to do but flop down on the shabby little couch and howl. So Della did it. Which instigates the moral reflection that life is made up of sobs, sniffles, and smiles, with sniffles predominating.

While the mistress of the home is gradually subsiding from the first stage to the second, take a look at the home. A furnished flat at $8 per week. It did not exactly beggar description, but it certainly had that word on the lookout for the mendicancy squad.

In the vestibule below was a letter-box into which no letter would go, and an electric button from which ​no mortal finger could coax a ring. Also appertaining thereunto was a card bearing the name “Mr. James Dillingham Young.”

The “Dillingham” had been flung to the breeze during a former period of prosperity when its possessor was being paid $30 per week. Now, when the income was shrunk to $20, the letters of “Dillingham” looked blurred, as though they were thinking seriously of contracting to a modest and unassuming D. But whenever Mr. James Dillingham Young came home and reached his flat above he was called “Jim” and greatly hugged by Mrs. James Dillingham Young, already introduced to you as Della. Which is all very good.

Della finished her cry and attended to her cheeks with the powder rag. She stood by the window and looked out dully at a grey cat walking a grey fence in a grey backyard. To-morrow would be Christmas Day, and she had only $1.87 with which to buy Jim a present. She had been saving every penny she could for months, with this result. Twenty dollars a week doesn’t go far. Expenses had been greater than she had calculated. They always are. Only $1.87 to buy a present for Jim. Her Jim. Many a happy hour she had spent planning for something nice for him. Something fine and rare and ​sterling—something just a little bit near to being worthy of the honour of being owned by Jim.

There was a pier-glass between the windows of the room. Perhaps you have seen a pier-glass in an $8 flat. A very thin and very agile person may, by observing his reflection in a rapid sequence of longitudinal strips, obtain a fairly accurate conception of his looks. Della, being slender, had mastered the art.

Suddenly she whirled from the window and stood before the glass. Her eyes were shining brilliantly, but her face had lost its colour within twenty seconds. Rapidly she pulled down her hair and let it fall to its full length.

Now, there were two possessions of the James Dillingham Youngs in which they both took a mighty pride. One was Jim’s gold watch that had been his father’s and his grandfather’s. The other was Della’s hair. Had the Queen of Sheba lived in the flat across the airshaft, Della would have let her hair hang out the window some day to dry just to depreciate Her Majesty’s jewels and gifts. Had King Solomon been the janitor, with all his treasures piled up in the basement, Jim would have pulled out his watch every time he passed, just to see him pluck at his beard from envy.

​So now Della’s beautiful hair fell about her, rippling and shining like a cascade of brown waters. It reached below her knee and made itself almost a garment for her. And then she did it up again nervously and quickly. Once she faltered for a minute and stood still while a tear or two splashed on the worn red carpet.

On went her old brown jacket; on went her old brown hat. With a whirl of skirts and with the brilliant sparkle still in her eyes, she fluttered out the door and down the stairs to the street.

Where she stopped the sign read: “Mme. Sofronie. Hair Goods of All Kinds.” One flight up Della ran, and collected herself, panting. Madame, large, too white, chilly, hardly looked the “Sofronie.”

“Will you buy my hair?” asked Della.

“I buy hair,” said Madame. “Take yer hat off and let’s have a sight at the looks of it.”

Down rippled the brown cascade.

“Twenty dollars,” said Madame, lifting the mass with a practised hand.

“Give it to me quick,” said Della,

Oh, and the next two hours tripped by on rosy wings. Forget the hashed metaphor. She was ransacking the stores for Jim’s present.

She found it at last. It surely had been made for ​Jim and no one else. There was no other like it in any of the stores, and she had turned all of them inside out. It was a platinum fob chain simple and chaste in design, properly proclaiming its value by substance alone and not by meretricious ornamentation—as all good things should do. It was even worthy of The Watch. As soon as she saw it she knew that it must be Jim’s. It was like him. Quietness and value—the description applied to both. Twenty-one dollars they took from her for it, and she hurried home with the 87 cents. With that chain on his watch Jim might be properly anxious about the time in any company. Grand as the watch was, he sometimes looked at it on the sly on account of the old leather strap that he used in place of a chain.

When Della reached home her intoxication gave way a little to prudence and reason. She got out her curling irons and lighted the gas and went to work repairing the ravages made by generosity added to love. Which is always a tremendous task, dear friends—a mammoth task.

Within forty minutes her head was covered with tiny, close-lying curls that made her look wonderfully like a truant schoolboy. She looked at her reflection in the mirror long, carefully, and critically.

​“If Jim doesn’t kill me,” she said to herself, “before he takes a second look at me, he’ll say I look like a Coney Island chorus girl. But what could I do—oh! what could I do with a dollar and eighty-seven cents?”

At 7 o’clock the coffee was made and the frying-pan was on the back of the stove hot and ready to cook the chops.

Jim was never late. Della doubled the fob chain in her hand and sat on the corner of the table near the door that he always entered. Then she heard his step on the stair away down on the first flight, and she turned white for just a moment. She had a habit of saying little silent prayers about the simplest everyday things, and now she whispered: “Please God, make him think I am still pretty.”

The door opened and Jim stepped in and closed it. He looked thin and very serious. Poor fellow, he was only twenty-two—and to be burdened with a family! He needed a new overcoat and he was without gloves.

Jim stopped inside the door, as immovable as a setter at the scent of quail. His eyes were fixed upon Della, and there was an expression in them that she could not read, and it terrified her. It was not anger, nor surprise, nor disapproval, nor horror, ​nor any of the sentiments that she had been prepared for. He simply stared at her fixedly with that peculiar expression on his face.

Della wriggled off the table and went for him.

“Jim, darling,” she cried, “don’t look at me that way. I had my hair cut off and sold it because I couldn’t have lived through Christmas without giving you a present. It’ll grow out again—you won’t mind, will you? I just had to do it. My hair grows awfully fast. Say ‘Merry Chistmas!’ Jim, and let’s be happy. You don’t know what a nice—what a beautiful, nice gift I’ve got for you.”

“You’ve cut off your hair?” asked Jim, laboriously, as if he had not arrived at that patent fact yet even after the hardest mental labour.

“Cut it off and sold it,” said Della. “Don’t you like me just as well, anyhow? I’m me without my hair, ain’t I?”

Jim looked about the room curiously.

“You say your hair is gone?” he said, with an air almost of idiocy.

“You needn’t look for it,” said Della. “It’s sold, I tell you—sold and gone, too. It’s Christmas Eve, boy. Be good to me, for it went for you. While the mistress of the home is gradually subsiding from the first stage to the second, take a look at the home. A furnished flat at $8 per week. It did not exactly beggar description, but it certainly had that word on the lookout for the mendicancy squad.

In the vestibule below was a letter-box into which no letter would go, and an electric button from which ​no mortal finger could coax a ring. Also appertaining thereunto was a card bearing the name “Mr. James Dillingham Young.”

The “Dillingham” had been flung to the breeze during a former period of prosperity when its possessor was being paid $30 per week. Now, when the income was shrunk to $20, the letters of “Dillingham” looked blurred, as though they were thinking seriously of contracting to a modest and unassuming D. But whenever Mr. James Dillingham Young came home and reached his flat above he was called “Jim” and greatly hugged by Mrs. James Dillingham Young, already introduced to you as Della. Which is all very good.

Della finished her cry and attended to her cheeks with the powder rag. She stood by the window and looked out dully at a grey cat walking a grey fence in a grey backyard. To-morrow would be Christmas Day, and she had only $1.87 with which to buy Jim a present. She had been saving every penny she could for months, with this result. Twenty dollars a week doesn’t go far. Expenses had been greater than she had calculated. They always are. Only $1.87 to buy a present for Jim. Her Jim. Many a happy hour she had spent planning for something nice for him. Something fine and rare and ​sterling—something just a little bit near to being worthy of the honour of being owned by Jim.

There was a pier-glass between the windows of the room. Perhaps you have seen a pier-glass in an $8 flat. A very thin and very agile person may, by observing his reflection in a rapid sequence of longitudinal strips, obtain a fairly accurate conception of his looks. Della, being slender, had mastered the art.

Suddenly she whirled from the window and stood before the glass. Her eyes were shining brilliantly, but her face had lost its colour within twenty seconds. Rapidly she pulled down her hair and let it fall to its full length.

Now, there were two possessions of the James Dillingham Youngs in which they both took a mighty pride. One was Jim’s gold watch that had been his father’s and his grandfather’s. The other was Della’s hair. Had the Queen of Sheba lived in the flat across the airshaft, Della would have let her hair hang out the window some day to dry just to depreciate Her Majesty’s jewels and gifts. Had King Solomon been the janitor, with all his treasures piled up in the basement, Jim would have pulled out his watch every time he passed, just to see him pluck at his beard from envy.

​So now Della’s beautiful hair fell about her, rippling and shining like a cascade of brown waters. It reached below her knee and made itself almost a garment for her. And then she did it up again nervously and quickly. Once she faltered for a minute and stood still while a tear or two splashed on the worn red carpet.

On went her old brown jacket; on went her old brown hat. With a whirl of skirts and with the brilliant sparkle still in her eyes, she fluttered out the door and down the stairs to the street.

Where she stopped the sign read: “Mme. Sofronie. Hair Goods of All Kinds.” One flight up Della ran, and collected herself, panting. Madame, large, too white, chilly, hardly looked the “Sofronie.”

“Will you buy my hair?” asked Della.

“I buy hair,” said Madame. “Take yer hat off and let’s have a sight at the looks of it.”

Down rippled the brown cascade.

“Twenty dollars,” said Madame, lifting the mass with a practised hand.

“Give it to me quick,” said Della,

Oh, and the next two hours tripped by on rosy wings. Forget the hashed metaphor. She was ransacking the stores for Jim’s present.

She found it at last. It surely had been made for ​Jim and no one else. There was no other like it in any of the stores, and she had turned all of them inside out. It was a platinum fob chain simple and chaste in design, properly proclaiming its value by substance alone and not by meretricious ornamentation—as all good things should do. It was even worthy of The Watch. As soon as she saw it she knew that it must be Jim’s. It was like him. Quietness and value—the description applied to both. Twenty-one dollars they took from her for it, and she hurried home with the 87 cents. With that chain on his watch Jim might be properly anxious about the time in any company. Grand as the watch was, he sometimes looked at it on the sly on account of the old leather strap that he used in place of a chain.

Jim was never late. Della doubled the fob chain in her hand and sat on the corner of the table near the door that he always entered. She had a habit of saying little silent prayers about the simplest everyday things, and now she whispered: “Please God, make him think I am still pretty.”

The door opened and Jim stepped in and closed it. He looked thin and very serious. Poor fellow, he was only twenty-two—and to be burdened with a family! He needed a new overcoat and he was without gloves.

“Isn’t it a dandy, Jim? I hunted all over town to find it. You’ll have to look at the time a hundred times a day now. Give me your watch. I want to see how it looks on it.”

Baseline

Widely available

This feature is well established and works across many devices and browser versions. It’s been available across browsers since July 2015.

  • See full compatibility
  • Learn more

The <article> HTML element represents a self-contained composition in a document, page, application, or site, which is intended to be independently distributable or reusable (e.g., in syndication). Examples include: a forum post, a magazine or newspaper article, or a blog entry, a product card, a user-submitted comment, an interactive widget or gadget, or any other independent item of content.

Try it

<article class="forecast">
  <h1>Weather forecast for Seattle</h1>
  <article class="day-forecast">
    <h2>03 March 2018</h2>
    <p>Rain.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="day-forecast">
    <h2>04 March 2018</h2>
    <p>Periods of rain.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="day-forecast">
    <h2>05 March 2018</h2>
    <p>Heavy rain.</p>
  </article>
</article>

.forecast {
  margin: 0;
  padding: 0.3rem;
  background-color: #eeeeee;
}

.forecast > h1,
.day-forecast {
  margin: 0.5rem;
  padding: 0.3rem;
  font-size: 1.2rem;
}

.day-forecast {
  background: right/contain content-box border-box no-repeat
    url("/shared-assets/images/examples/rain.svg") white;
}

.day-forecast > h2,
.day-forecast > p {
  margin: 0.2rem;
  font-size: 1rem;
}

Attributes

This element only includes the global attributes.

Usage notes

A given document can have multiple articles in it; for example, on a blog that shows the text of each article one after another as the reader scrolls, each post would be contained in an <article> element, possibly with one or more <section>s within.

  • Each <article> should be identified, typically by including a heading (<h1> - <h6> element) as a child of the <article> element.
  • When an <article> element is nested, the inner element represents an article related to the outer element. For example, the comments of a blog post can be <article> elements nested in the <article> representing the blog post.
  • Author information of an <article> element can be provided through the <address> element, but it doesn't apply to nested <article> elements.
  • The publication date and time of an <article> element can be described using the datetime attribute of a <time> element.

Examples

html

<article class="film_review">
  <h2>Jurassic Park</h2>
  <section class="main_review">
    <h3>Review</h3>
    <p>Dinos were great!</p>
  </section>
  <section class="user_reviews">
    <h3>User reviews</h3>
    <article class="user_review">
      <h4>Too scary!</h4>
      <p>Way too scary for me.</p>
      <footer>
        <p>
          Posted on
          <time datetime="2015-05-16 19:00">May 16</time>
          by Lisa.
        </p>
      </footer>
    </article>
    <article class="user_review">
      <h4>Love the dinos!</h4>
      <p>I agree, dinos are my favorite.</p>
      <footer>
        <p>
          Posted on
          <time datetime="2015-05-17 19:00">May 17</time>
          by Tom.
        </p>
      </footer>
    </article>
  </section>
  <footer>
    <p>
      Posted on
      <time datetime="2015-05-15 19:00">May 15</time>
      by Staff.
    </p>
  </footer>
</article>

Result

  • Other section-related elements: <body>, <nav>, <section>, <aside>, h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, <hgroup>, <header>, <footer>, <address>
